source.title: Effect of pre-training scale on intra- and inter-domain, full and few-shot transfer learning for natural and X-Ray chest images

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary material are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how model and pre-training data scale affect held-out transfer performance in natural and medical image domains, extending scale-related generalization evidence to cross-domain transfer.
record.gate_note: The study reports held-out transfer metrics under varied pre-training model sizes, source datasets, and transfer targets. It does not test random-label memorization, interpolation thresholds, architecture comparisons, optimizer comparisons, batch-size effects, dropout, sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. None of the listed versions is directly tested.
record.test_reason: The study measures transfer performance after varying pre-training model size, source-data size and domain. None of V1–V8 is tested. In particular, comparing two ResNets that differ in both depth and width, without measuring training error or locating interpolation, does not test V2. Using a large-batch training recipe does not test V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors conclude that larger pre-training scale benefits natural-to-natural transfer in full- and few-shot regimes and medical-to-medical transfer chiefly in full-shot settings. Natural-to-medical improvements are clear for large targets with full-shot fine-tuning, but inconsistent for small targets or few-shot transfer. They also emphasize that the largest ImageNet-21k model matches or outperforms models pre-trained on the largest available medical supersets for large medical targets.
record.recipe_differences: Supervised pre-training and fine-tuning for transfer, with SGD plus adaptive gradient clipping; the original claim versions concern other training interventions and generalization measures.
record.method_sensitivity: Held-out transfer performance varies with pre-training model size, source-data scale and domain, target size, and full-shot versus few-shot regime. Hyperparameter selection uses BiT-HyperRule; the authors note that tuning or changing the rule could alter results.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger pre-training models and datasets generally improve natural-to-natural transfer and full-shot medical-to-medical transfer. Natural-to-medical benefits are consistent for large targets in full-shot transfer, but not for small targets or few-shot transfer. The largest ImageNet-21k model matches or exceeds medical-source models on large medical targets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benefits of supervised pre-training scale for transfer depend on source and target domains, target-data size and the number of fine-tuning examples.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Joint Conference on Neural Network; short version published in MedNeurIPS 2021, long version in IJCNN 2022
record.problems: The study uses only ResNet architectures and supervised classification, does not explore scales beyond ImageNet-21k or substantially larger open medical datasets, and relies on BiT-HyperRule rather than task-specific hyperparameter tuning. The authors report relatively large variance in few-shot runs. It studies transfer test performance rather than train-test error gaps.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 includes medical targets and all four natural-pretraining model/source-scale combinations; the natural-target transfer results in Table 2 are omitted to keep within the 60-row limit and because they do not add a distinct claim-version test. Few-shot figure-only transfer values are omitted because the plots provide no tabulated numeric values; the text-level findings are summarized in authors_conclusion and fits_no_version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed for zero training error; no interpolation threshold or convergence-based width sweep is measured.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity; only ResNets are evaluated.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; adaptive gradient clipping is not an adaptive-optimizer comparison.
Held-out performance across batch sizes under matched epoch budgets and the effects of adapting the training recipe.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence and removal of dropout with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps and comparisons with norm- or margin-based measures.
Removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples followed by retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All 44 numerical values match Tables 2 and 5. Their states are changed to cannot_determine relative to V1–V8, rather than treating transfer gains as observations of those versions. The distributed-training supplement reports throughput and an accuracy sanity check, without a comparative held-out batch-size result testing V5. The rows_left_out statement incorrectly says natural-target results were omitted: R1–R16 contain them. Medical-source comparisons are instead absent from the rows, but do not bear on V1–V8. E2 exceeds the requested quote length and should be shortened or paraphrased.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of natural-label and random-label test accuracy.
No width sweep around the zero-training-error threshold, and no training-error results for the reported transfer runs.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No sharpness or other generalization-measure comparison.
No removal of memorized training examples.
